---
title: "Your own research guide"
---

Six research boxes are behind you. Every one of them ended the same way. You
picked a source and typed something into it. Then you did something with what
came back. That is a method, and it is already yours. Most people never write theirs
down, so it stays a habit they cannot look at and cannot improve. Today you
write it down.

## Write your research guide {#sec-research-guide-task}

Write your personal research guide in your own words, between 150 and 300
words. English or German, whichever you think in. Write it in the first person,
and describe what you actually do rather than what a good student would do. A
guide that admits you ask an AI first is worth more to you than one that claims
you open MDN first when you don't.

Answer these while you write:

* Which of the three sources you reach for first, and what makes you switch to
  another one.
* When you open MDN Web Docs, and what you do once the page is in front of you.
* Which AI you actually use. Name it.
* What you type in each place. One real example you remember beats a rule.
* How you check something an AI told you before you build on it.
* What you write down afterwards, and where that note ends up.

The last one carries the most weight. Your exam runs on a computer with no
internet and no AI, with your own course material allowed, so whatever you
wrote down in your own words during the year is what walks into that room with
you.

## How the writing activity works {#sec-research-guide-activity}

The link at the end of this chapter opens a writing activity on novedu, and it
gives you two panes. You write your guide on one side. On the other side sits
an AI coach that reads whatever stands in the editor at that moment and talks
to you about it. It can ask you about a sentence and it can tell you a sentence
is vague, but it has no way to type into your draft. Every word in the guide
stays yours.

Write a few sentences, ask the coach what is still unclear, then keep writing.
When the guide says what you wanted it to say, press Save.

This activity is not anonymous, so your teacher reads what you saved, with your
name on it. Nobody grades your research habits and there are no points here.
Your teacher reads the guides to learn how this class really works, and to have
something concrete to talk about with you in the next lesson.

## There is no correct guide {#sec-research-guide-no-right-answer}

Two people in your class can write guides that contradict each other, and both
can be good. Your order of sources is yours. How much you lean on an AI is
yours. The coach will not argue with any of that.

What the coach does instead is push for detail. It quotes your own words back
at you and asks the question the sentence left open. You write "I just google
it", and it wants to know what you typed the last time and what you did with
the first result. One or two questions per turn, and then it is your move
again.

The coach steps in with a correction in one case, which is a claim in your
draft that is simply wrong. What MDN is and who writes it, what an AI chat can
and cannot see, what you are allowed to bring into the exam: those are facts,
not preferences. The coach says so briefly and then goes back to asking
questions.

## Keep it {#sec-research-guide-keep}

Save the text, and keep your own copy of it somewhere you will find again. A
later chapter of this book asks you to open this guide and look at what has
changed.
